say.text: Last stop: twelve mixed stems, none seen earlier in this module. Hints are on for the first six; the last six are unaided.
A registrar's note reads: 'Ultrasound is the most sensitive and specific test for acute cholecystitis, so a positive scan needs nothing more.'
Which correction is right?

choices.label: Ultrasound is right; it is the most sensitive and specific test
Ultrasound first; HIDA scan is the most sensitive and specific
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Split the question in two: which test you order first, and which test answers 'most sensitive and specific'.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because ultrasound is the first test you order, but first-line and most sensitive and specific are different questions.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate 'first investigation' from 'confirming investigation' before the next stem.

say.text: Yes. Ultrasound is the first investigation for gallstones and suspected cholecystitis. A HIDA scan is the most sensitive and specific: non-filling of the gallbladder with tracer reaching the duodenum confirms cystic duct obstruction.
Before surgery, a 58-year-old man has a bilirubin of 4 mg/dL, a dilated duct on ultrasound and gallstones in his gallbladder.
You want to see the bile duct without passing a scope into it. Which test?

choices.label: Diagnostic ERCP, since it can also clear the stone
MRCP, magnetic resonance imaging of the bile ducts
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which test needs a scope passed into the duodenum, and which one only images the duct.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because ERCP both finds and clears a duct stone, but the question asks for a look taken before any instrument goes in.

sure_note.text: You were sure: ERCP is diagnostic and therapeutic, so it is kept for a stone that is already likely.

say.text: Yes. MRCP is the non-invasive investigation of choice for common bile duct stones. ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic, so it is reserved for when a stone is likely.
A 46-year-old woman has had 30 hours of right upper pain. Her WBC is 13,500/mm³, she has no organ dysfunction and no palpable mass.
Her registrar says the WBC alone makes her TG18 Grade II. Which is right?

choices.label: Grade II: a WBC above 12,000/mm³ meets the criterion
Grade I: her WBC is under the Grade II threshold
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Check the WBC against the TG18 figure for Grade II, not against the routine laboratory upper limit.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because 12,000 is the familiar routine laboratory cut-off, but TG18 grades use their own figures, and they sit higher.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the grade's own criteria rather than a lab cut-off you already know.

say.text: Yes. TG18 Grade I is acute cholecystitis that meets neither the Grade II nor the Grade III criteria. Her WBC is below the Grade II figure, and her pain and organ status do not qualify her higher.
A registrar, reviewing a Grade III patient on noradrenaline, says the grade does not change the operation.
Which plan is correct for this patient?

choices.label: Operate at once; remove the source of sepsis
Support organs and drain the gallbladder first
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a patient in organ failure can survive on the table, and what the grade is there to tell you.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because removing the gallbladder seems to remove the sepsis, but in organ failure the patient must be stabilised before any operation.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link the grade to the order of steps, not only to the operation.

say.text: Yes. In Grade III, organ support comes first and the gallbladder is drained. Surgery is deferred until the patient is fit, because the operation itself is unsafe while organs are failing.
An exam item asks about a fit patient with acute calculous cholecystitis, and gives both a PYQ key and current practice.
Which statement pairs the two correctly?

choices.label: PYQs expected early surgery; current practice is interval surgery
PYQs expected interval surgery; current practice is early surgery
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Work out which of the two plans the older exam key used, and which one a fit patient gets today.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because the older plan of waiting is the one many notes carry, but the two columns have been swapped against each other.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which column each plan belongs to before you commit.

say.text: Yes. PYQs have expected conservative care then interval cholecystectomy at 6 to 8 weeks. Current practice in a fit patient is early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission, which shortens stay without more complications.
A 40-year-old woman has gallstones on a screening ultrasound done for a thyroid problem. She has never had pain, fever or jaundice.
What is the sensible plan?

choices.label: Remove the gallbladder now; stones can lead to cancer
Observe; the yearly risk of symptoms is low
Ursodeoxycholic acid tablets to dissolve the stones
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what these stones have actually done in this patient, and what the usual yearly risk is for silent stones.
That is not the right choice.
It tempts because stones are linked to cancer and cholecystitis, but that link belongs to symptomatic disease or a special risk feature, not to every silent stone.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a silent stone is not an indication for surgery unless a high-risk feature is present.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because ursodeoxycholic acid is the usual dissolution drug, but it works only for a particular stone in a particular gallbladder, and this patient has no indication to treat.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so recall the stone and gallbladder conditions that dissolution needs.

say.text: Yes. Most gallstones never cause symptoms, and the risk of symptoms is about 1 to 2 per cent a year, so silent stones need no treatment unless a special feature is present.
At laparoscopy, the cystic duct holds an impacted stone, and the common hepatic duct is narrowed where the two run side by side.
Which name fits?

choices.label: Choledocholithiasis, a stone lying inside the bile duct
Mirizzi syndrome, from a stone pressing on the duct

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because a duct stone is the usual cause of obstructive jaundice, but check where the stone in this stem actually lies before you name it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the site of the stone before naming the syndrome.

say.text: Yes. Mirizzi syndrome is a stone in Hartmann's pouch or the cystic duct compressing the common hepatic duct. Choledocholithiasis is a stone inside the common bile duct itself.
A gallstone impacted in the duodenum blocks the outlet of the stomach, and the patient vomits without passing food.
Which name covers this?

choices.label: Gallstone ileus, a stone lodged in the terminal ileum
Bouveret's syndrome, gastric outlet obstruction by a stone

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because gallstone ileus is the better-known stone obstruction, but the site and the presentation here point to the stomach outlet, not the small bowel.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so match the name to where the stone lodges before you commit.

say.text: Yes. Bouveret's syndrome is gastric outlet obstruction from a stone impacted in the duodenum or pylorus. Gallstone ileus is small-bowel obstruction, most often lodged in the terminal ileum.
Charcot's triad in cholangitis is fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper pain. Reynolds' pentad adds two findings.
Which two are added?

choices.label: Rigors and hypotension, the sepsis signs
Hypotension and confusion, from sepsis and the brain

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because rigors is the sepsis sign people remember, but rigors is already a triad item, so it cannot be one of the two added findings.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check which findings are already in the triad before you add any.

say.text: Yes. Reynolds' pentad is Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion, which reflect the sepsis and the cerebral effects of cholangitis.
A gallbladder with infected bile, and the plain film shows no gas in the wall or the lumen.
Which organism is most often grown from this bile?

choices.label: Clostridium perfringens, a gas-forming organism of bile
Escherichia coli, the commonest organism in infected bile

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because Clostridium is the organism linked to gas in the gallbladder, but the film here shows no gas, so the gas-forming picture does not apply.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a gas-forming organism belongs with gas in the wall, and that is not this picture.

say.text: Yes. E. coli is the commonest organism in infected bile. Clostridium perfringens is the typical organism of emphysematous cholecystitis, where gas is seen in the wall or lumen.
A junior asks which step most prevents the commonest major bile duct injury at laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Which answer do you give?

choices.label: Confirm two structures entering the gallbladder, then clip
Confirm the critical view of safety before any clip
Control any bleeding from the cystic artery first

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because 'two structures' is the memorable part of the view, but counting structures alone does not show that the duct has been identified.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-check which requirement of the view you were relying on.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because bleeding is the most feared event at this operation, but feared is not the same as commonest; check what usually goes wrong with the duct itself.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask which error is most common, not which event is most dramatic.

say.text: Yes. The critical view needs the triangle cleared, the lower gallbladder separated from the cystic plate, and two structures seen entering it. Misidentification of the common bile duct is the commonest cause of major injury.
A 64-year-old on a ventilator has septic shock from pneumonia. Ultrasound shows acalculous cholecystitis, and he is too unwell for an operation.
What is the treatment of choice for the gallbladder?

choices.label: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy, as for any cholecystitis
Percutaneous cholecystostomy to drain the gallbladder

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It tempts because the operation is the usual answer for cholecystitis, but the stem names critical illness, and that changes who can safely have surgery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the patient is fit for surgery before you choose the operation.

say.text: Yes. Acalculous cholecystitis in critically ill patients is treated by drainage when surgery is unsafe. Percutaneous cholecystostomy is used for patients too ill or high-risk for surgery.

cards.q: Most sensitive and specific test for acute cholecystitis, and the first test?
cards.a: HIDA scan is the most sensitive and specific; non-filling of the gallbladder confirms cystic duct obstruction. Ultrasound is the first test.

cards.q: Non-invasive investigation of choice for common bile duct stones?
cards.a: MRCP. ERCP is both diagnostic and therapeutic, so it is kept for when a stone is likely.

cards.q: What makes TG18 Grade I acute cholecystitis?
cards.a: Disease that meets neither the Grade II nor the Grade III criteria; a WBC below the Grade II figure does not make it Grade II.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for a fit patient with acute calculous cholecystitis?
cards.a: Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the index admission, ideally within 72 hours of onset.

cards.q: Silent gallstones: what is the usual plan?
cards.a: Observation. Symptoms develop at about 1 to 2 per cent a year, and dissolution works only for small radiolucent cholesterol stones with a working gallbladder.
Mirizzi: a stone in Hartmann's pouch or the cystic duct compresses the common hepatic duct. Choledocholithiasis: a stone inside the common bile duct.

cards.q: Critical view of safety, and the commonest cause of major bile duct injury?
cards.a: Triangle cleared, lower gallbladder separated, two structures seen. Misidentification of the common bile duct is the commonest cause.
